---
title: "Vitest: tests that read like sentences"
---

Your bracelet project has two green tests in `src/bracelet.test.ts`. Two tests
say very little about a model whose whole job is refusing the wrong move, so
this chapter grows that file into one test per rule. It starts with a test that
goes red for a reason that has nothing to do with the bracelet.

## A test that fails before it checks anything {#sec-vitest-experiment}

Open `homework/bracelet-tests` and start the watcher:

```bash
npm run test:watch
```

Vitest runs the file once, prints the same summary as `npm test`, and then
stays open:

```
 PASS  Waiting for file changes...
       press h to show help, press q to quit
```

Leave it running. Add one line to the imports at the top of
`src/bracelet.test.ts`:

```ts
import { RuleError } from './rule-error';
```

Then add a third test inside the `describe`, and save:

```ts
  it('rejects a second letter in a row', () => {
    const bracelet = new Bracelet();
    bracelet.addLetter('A');

    expect(bracelet.addLetter('B')).toThrow(RuleError);
  });
```

The watcher notices the save, runs the file again, and turns red:

```
 FAIL  src/bracelet.test.ts > Bracelet > rejects a second letter in a row
RuleError: You need to add a spacer bead next!
 ❯ Bracelet.addLetter src/bracelet.ts:16:13
 ❯ src/bracelet.test.ts:23:21
```

The bracelet did exactly what you wanted. It refused the second letter and threw
a `RuleError`, and the test still failed. TypeScript had nothing to complain
about either, so the red run is the only place this shows up.

## Why toThrow needs an arrow function {#sec-vitest-tothrow}

`expect(bracelet.addLetter('B'))` is an ordinary function call with an argument,
so the argument is computed first. `addLetter` throws while the argument is
being computed, the exception walks out of your `it` block, and `expect` never
runs at all. Vitest catches the exception and reports the test as failed,
because a test that throws is a test that failed.

Hand `expect` a function instead of a value:

```ts
    expect(() => bracelet.addLetter('B')).toThrow(RuleError);
```

Now the call sits inside an arrow function, and nothing has run yet when
`expect` gets it. `toThrow(RuleError)` calls that arrow function itself, catches
what comes out, and checks that it is a `RuleError`. Save, and the watcher goes
green:

```
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  3 passed (3)
```

The value goes into `expect` when you check a result, and the call goes into an
arrow function when you check a refusal.

## toBe compares, toEqual looks inside {#sec-vitest-matchers}

`toBe` compares the way `===` does, which is what you want for a number, a
string, or a boolean. Try it on the items of a fresh bracelet:

```ts
    expect(bracelet.items).toBe([]);
```

```
AssertionError: expected [] to be [] // Object.is equality

If it should pass with deep equality, replace "toBe" with "toStrictEqual"

Expected: []
Received: serializes to the same string
```

Two empty arrays print the same and are still two different objects, and `===`
compares objects by identity, not by content. The `items` getter makes that
certain: it hands out a copy of the array, so it can never give you the same
array you typed into the test.

`toEqual` walks into the array and compares what is in it:

```ts
    expect(bracelet.items).toEqual([]);
```

That passes. Take `toBe` for a number, a string, or a boolean, and `toEqual` for
an array or an object. `toStrictEqual` is a stricter relative you will not need
this year.

## A fresh bracelet for every test {#sec-vitest-beforeeach}

Every test so far starts with `const bracelet = new Bracelet();`. Eight tests
would repeat that line eight times, and one shared bracelet instead would make
the tests eat each other: test three finds whatever test two pushed onto it, and
passes or fails depending on the order the tests run in.

`beforeEach` runs a piece of setup before every single `it` in its `describe`:

```ts
describe('Bracelet', () => {
  let bracelet: Bracelet;

  beforeEach(() => {
    bracelet = new Bracelet();
  });

  it('starts with no items', () => {
    expect(bracelet.items).toEqual([]);
  });
});
```

`let bracelet: Bracelet;` without a value is the one place this course writes a
`let` like that. The value cannot be given here, because a new one is needed for
every test, and `beforeEach` fills it in before any `it` body starts. Add
`beforeEach` to the names you import from `'vitest'`, and let
`npm run check:fix` sort that list for you.

## Arrange, act, assert {#sec-vitest-aaa}

A test reads best in three blocks with a blank line between them: build the
situation, do the one thing you are testing, then check the result.

```ts
  it('warns when a spacer of another color joins', () => {
    bracelet.addLetter('A');
    bracelet.addSpacer('#f4a0a0');
    bracelet.addLetter('B');

    const warning = bracelet.addSpacer('#a0d4a0');

    expect(warning).toBe('You are mixing spacer colors!');
  });
```

Arrange builds a bracelet that already carries one bead. Act adds a bead in a
second color. Assert names the exact text that comes back. Keep one behavior per `it`: a
test with three unrelated checks in it tells you that something is wrong and
makes you guess which of the three.

The name after `it` is a sentence that starts with the word "it", written in
lowercase. `it('rejects a second letter in a row', ...)` reads as "it rejects a
second letter in a row", and that sentence is what Vitest prints when the test
fails.

## Reading a failure {#sec-vitest-failure}

A test that expects `'You are mixing spacer colors'`, without the exclamation
mark at the end, fails like this:

```
 FAIL  src/bracelet.test.ts > Bracelet > warns when a spacer of another color joins
AssertionError: expected 'You are mixing spacer colors!' to be 'You are mixing spacer colors' // Object.is equality

Expected: "You are mixing spacer colors"
Received: "You are mixing spacer colors!"

 ❯ src/bracelet.test.ts:40:21
     38|     const warning = bracelet.addSpacer('#a0d4a0');
     39|
     40|     expect(warning).toBe('You are mixing spacer colors');
       |                     ^
     41|   });
     42|
```

Four things are worth finding in there. The `FAIL` line names the file, then the
`describe`, then the `it`, separated by `>`. The `AssertionError` line says what
came back and what you asked for, in that order. `Expected` is your text and
`Received` is the model's, so here the bug sits in the test, not in the
bracelet. The `❯` line is the address: file, line number, column number, with
the source underneath and a caret under the matcher that failed. Ctrl-click that
address in the VS Code terminal to jump to the line, and expect your own numbers
to differ from the ones above.

## Run once, or keep running {#sec-vitest-run-watch}

`npm test` runs every test file once and exits, and its exit code says whether
everything passed. That is the form a build server needs, and the next chapter
uses it.

`npm run test:watch` is the one to keep open in a second terminal while you
write tests. It reruns on every save, works on the files your change affects,
and quits when you press `q`.

::: {.callout-note}
## Tests inside VS Code

VS Code has a Vitest extension that puts a run button next to every `it`.
Install it if you like it. This course stays in the terminal, because `npm test`
works on every machine, including the school computer you sit at during an
exam.
:::

::: {.research title="Four things this chapter leaves to you"}
The two exercises below check a value that is `undefined`, count the items on a
bracelet, compare two euro amounts that do not match to the last digit, and park
one test you have not written yet. All four live on the `expect` page of the
[Vitest documentation](https://vitest.dev/api/expect), and vitest.dev is the
site to search here, not MDN.

1. `addSpacer` returns `undefined` when it has nothing to warn about. Which
   matcher checks exactly that, and which matcher checks the opposite?
2. Which matcher checks how many items an array holds, without reading
   `.length` yourself, and what other kind of value can you use it on?
3. A walk of 3 km pays `3 * 0.38`, and JavaScript computes
   `1.1400000000000001` for that, so `toBe(1.14)` fails. Which matcher compares
   two numbers that are close enough, and what does its second argument decide?
4. You know a behavior you want to test but you have not written the test yet.
   What does `it.todo('refuses a negative distance')` do when the tests run, and
   how does the summary line count it?

For the exam, the matcher for `undefined` and the matcher for a length have to
be in your head. Almost every test file you write by hand needs both.
:::

## Exercise A: every rule of the bracelet {#sec-vitest-exercise-bracelet}

1. In `homework/bracelet-tests`, rewrite `src/bracelet.test.ts`. It holds one
   `describe('Bracelet', ...)`, a `let bracelet: Bracelet;` with a `beforeEach`
   that gives it a new bracelet, and eight `it` blocks written as arrange, act,
   assert. Use two different color strings where you need them, for example
   `'#f4a0a0'` and `'#a0d4a0'`.

2. Write one test for each of these behaviors:

   * a new bracelet has no items
   * a letter cube and then a spacer bead leave two items on the bracelet
   * a second letter right after the first throws a `RuleError`
   * a spacer bead on an empty bracelet throws a `RuleError`
   * a spacer bead in a second color gives back
     `'You are mixing spacer colors!'`
   * one more spacer bead in another color after that gives back nothing,
     because the warning comes only once
   * `removeLast()` on an empty bracelet leaves it empty
   * `removeLast()` after a letter cube and a spacer bead leaves one item

3. Where a test counts items, use the matcher from the research task instead of
   reading `.length` yourself. Its message prints the array and both lengths
   when the test goes red, which `toBe` on a number cannot do.

4. Write the tests one at a time with the watcher running, and know why each one
   is red or green before you start the next.

5. Run `npm test`. Expected result:

   ```
    Test Files  1 passed (1)
         Tests  8 passed (8)
   ```

6. Break one rule in `src/bracelet.ts` on purpose, for example by letting
   `addLetter` push without asking, and run `npm test` again. Read which test
   names turn up under `Failed Tests`, then put the rule back.

7. Run `npm run verify`, fix what it reports, and commit.

## Exercise B: what the trip is worth {#sec-vitest-exercise-travel}

The travel classes from the polymorphism chapter do arithmetic on a distance and
hand back numbers and strings, and not one of them touches the page, which makes
them easy to test.

{{< exercise travel-costs tests=true >}}

1. Create a new app from our tests template inside `coursework/`, in a folder
   called `travel-tests`.

2. Copy `travel.ts`, `car.ts`, `motorcycle.ts`, `bicycle.ts`, `walk.ts`, and
   `index.ts` from your travel project of the polymorphism chapter into `src/`.
   Delete `src/math.ts` and `src/math.test.ts`.

3. Run `npm start`, type a distance, and click Car once. The line and the total
   appear as before, which tells you the copy is complete.

4. Create `src/travel.test.ts` with one `describe` per class: `Car`,
   `Motorcycle`, `Bicycle`, and `Walk`. Each class gets its objects built inside
   the tests, so no `beforeEach` is needed here.

5. Write one test per row of this table. Each one builds the travel with that
   distance and checks what `reimbursement()` gives back.

   | Travel | Distance in km | Reimbursement in euro |
   | --- | ---: | ---: |
   | Car, nobody along | 10 | 5 |
   | Car, 1 passenger | 10 | 5.15 |
   | Car, 2 passengers | 10 | 5.3 |
   | Motorcycle | 10 | 2.5 |
   | Bicycle | 10 | 2.5 |
   | Walk | 10 | 3.8 |
   | Bicycle | 1 | 0 |
   | Walk | 1 | 0 |
   | Walk | 3 | 1.14 |

6. One row of that table refuses to pass with `toBe`, and the research task
   names the matcher that gets it green. Two decimal places are enough.

7. Add one more test for `summary()`: a car over 10 km with nobody along gives
   back the string `'Car, 10.00 km: 5.00 €'`.

8. Add `it.todo('refuses a negative distance')` at the end of the `Walk` block.
   Nobody has written that rule yet, and the reminder belongs next to the tests
   rather than in your head.

9. Run `npm test`. Expected result:

   ```
    Test Files  1 passed (1)
         Tests  10 passed | 1 todo (11)
   ```

10. Run `npm run verify`, fix what it reports, and commit.

::: {.callout-tip}
## When you finish early

Give `Travel` a check that refuses a distance below zero, throwing an error of
its own the way the bracelet does. Then turn your `it.todo` into a real test
with `toThrow`, and watch the count in the summary move from todo to passed.
:::
